original_value: In many real-world sequential decision making problems, the number of available actions (decisions) can vary over time. While problems like catastrophic forgetting, changing transition dynamics, changing rewards functions, etc. have been well-studied in the lifelong learning literature, the setting where the size of the action set changes remains unaddressed. In this paper, we present first steps towards developing an algorithm that autonomously adapts to an action set whose size changes over time. To tackle this open problem, we break it into two problems that can be solved iteratively: inferring the underlying, unknown, structure in the space of actions and optimizing a policy that leverages this structure. We demonstrate the efficiency of this approach on large-scale real-world lifelong learning problems.

result.paraphrase: In many real-world sequential decision-making tasks, the number of actions available can change over time. Although issues such as catastrophic forgetting, shifting transition dynamics, and changing reward functions have been widely studied in lifelong learning, the case where the action set itself changes has not been addressed. In this paper, we take initial steps toward an algorithm that automatically adapts to an action set whose size varies over time. To address this open problem, we decompose it into two iteratively solvable subproblems: inferring the hidden structure in the action space and optimizing a policy that exploits that structure. We show the effectiveness of this method on large-scale real-world lifelong learning problems.
